title: Redis Deep Dive
description: Explore Redis data structures, persistence options, memory management, and pub/sub messaging capabilities.

segments.text: Redis is more than a cache. It's an in-memory data structure store that can serve as a database, message broker, and queue. It handles millions of operations per second with sub-millisecond latency. Let's see what makes it special.

Strings are the simplest Redis type. SET, GET, INCR, DECR. But 'string' is misleading — it can hold text, numbers, or even serialized objects up to five hundred twelve megabytes. Atomic increment makes it perfect for counters and rate limiters.

Hashes are like mini dictionaries inside a key. Perfect for representing objects — user colon forty-two with fields name, email, and age. You can get or set individual fields without touching the rest. Very memory-efficient for small objects.

Lists are linked lists — fast push and pop from both ends. Great for queues and activity feeds. Sets are unique collections with blazing fast membership checks. Sorted sets add a score to each member, perfect for leaderboards and priority queues.
These aren't just abstract data types — they're building blocks for real features. A sorted set becomes a leaderboard. A list becomes a job queue. A set becomes a 'who's online' tracker.
segments.thought_prompt: How would you use a Redis sorted set to implement a real-time trending hashtags feature?

segments.text: Redis is in-memory, but it can persist data. RDB snapshots take a point-in-time dump of the entire dataset at configured intervals. Fast to restore, compact to store, but you can lose data between snapshots if Redis crashes.

AOF — Append Only File — logs every write operation. It's more durable because you can configure it to sync every second or even every write. But the file grows large over time, so Redis rewrites it periodically to compact it.

Memory management is critical in Redis. Every key and value lives in RAM. The maxmemory setting caps usage. When the limit is hit, Redis applies your chosen eviction policy — LRU, LFU, random, or it can refuse new writes entirely.

Redis pub/sub lets clients subscribe to channels and receive messages in real time. A publisher sends a message to a channel, and all subscribers get it instantly. Perfect for chat, notifications, and live updates.

But pub/sub has no persistence — if a subscriber is offline when a message is sent, it's gone forever. For reliable messaging, use Redis Streams instead. Streams combine the pub/sub pattern with persistent, replayable message logs.

In production, Redis is often deployed with replication for high availability. A primary handles writes, replicas handle reads. Redis Sentinel or Redis Cluster manages automatic failover when the primary goes down.
segments.thought_prompt: Why might you choose Redis Cluster over Redis Sentinel for a large-scale deployment?

segments.text: Redis is a Swiss Army knife — strings for caching, hashes for objects, sorted sets for rankings, pub/sub for real-time messaging. Its speed comes from memory, and its flexibility comes from rich data structures. Next: cache invalidation, the hardest problem in computing.
